<Rep. Jared Huffman>: H.R. 5576 would amend the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970 by designating certain geothermal exploration projects as non-major federal actions, thereby exempting these activities from review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). The bill would also direct the Interior Secretary to designate areas of federal land for priority geothermal leasing. After the initial designations, the Secretary is also directed to prepare programmatic environmental impact statements (PEISs) for geothermal leasing. No additional NEPA analysis would be necessary for a lease sale of lands covered by such a PEIS for at least 10 years.
There are two primary concerns with this legislation.
First, rather than expediting permitting through a well-considered administrative NEPA categorical exclusion (CE), this bill would waive all NEPA review for certain exploration activities. It is far more appropriate for federal agencies to develop CEs rather than for members of Congress to create legislative exemptions to NEPA. Agencies use their technical expertise to ensure a proposed categorical exclusion has little to no environmental impact, and agencies may incorporate public feedback and define site-specific conditions where the CE may not apply.
In the final months of the Biden administration, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) finalized and adopted several CEs for geothermal exploration that preserve key safeguards that this legislation would eliminate, and the geothermal industry is utilizing these CEs effectively.
In contrast, the waiver in this legislation is highly specific--limited to test wells with a diameter of 13\3/8\ inches, a number that has changed each Congress as versions of this legislation have been introduced. Directing BLM to develop a more general CE would allow far more flexibility and offer essential protection in extraordinary circumstances.
Second, while Committee Democrats support efforts to identify priority areas for geothermal leasing and to conduct thorough programmatic environmental reviews, there are concerns about waiving all NEPA requirements for geothermal leasing following a PEIS. Eliminating lease-sale-level NEPA analysis would short-circuit the way PEISs work. Committee Democrats strongly support PEISs, as they take a broad look at an activity's impacts and can streamline more specific analysis at the lease-sale level. Lease sale-level analysis can draw on PEIS-level analysis and build upon it as needed to incorporate site-specific information and ensure decisions are legally and scientifically defensible.
Last Congress, this provision of the bill said, ``If the Secretary determines that the designation of a geothermal leasing priority area has been sufficiently analyzed by a programmatic environmental impact statement, the Secretary shall not prepare any additional analysis under [NEPA]'' for a specific area.
Now, the bill text says that the Secretary ``shall not prepare any additional analysis under [NEPA]'' for a specific area ``unless the Secretary determines there are substantial new circumstances or information'' about adverse effects (emphasis added). This change would establish a presumption against lease-sale analysis in many cases, even when site-specific risks, conflicts, or new information warrant it.
Democrats made several suggestions to amend the legislation to secure unanimous consent, but the majority declined to negotiate.
I oppose the legislation as written.
Jared Huffman,
Ranking Member.
